TITLE: Xylem Anomalies as Indicators of Maladaptation to Climate in Forest Trees: Implications for Assisted Migration
SPECIES: T1=Picea glauca (white spruce); T2=Pinus contorta; T3=Pinus nigra
CONTEXT: In this present study, we used a long-term provenance trial in Alberta, Canada to analyze xylem anomalies in 39-year old white spruce (Picea glauca [Moench] Voss) trees representing six ecozones. We hypothesized that xylem anomalies can be viewed as symptoms of maladaptation to local growing conditions, and that they can be used as a tool to guide seed transfer in the light of climate change. Specifically, we will interpret xylem anomalies in the light of the climate differences between the source environment of the provenance, and the test environment at the planting site. The trial site is located in the central boreal plains of western Canada, and supports a boreal mixedwood ecosystem on a clay-loam gray luvisol soil. The test site climate is cool and dry, with a mean annual temperature of 0.5°C and mean annual precipitation of 491 mm. Trees from 43 provenances across the Canadian species range were planted in 1982 as 4-year-old seedlings. The experimental design is a randomized complete block design with five blocks and five-tree row plots planted in each block with a 2.5 × 2.5 m spacing. We extracted a wood core from one tree of average height and DBH from each row plot, i.e. one core per block and provenance of the sampling design. Samples were collected during the summer of 2017, with 2016 being the last complete year used for analyses. For every core, we discarded the first few sections to avoid sampling tissue that could have been damage by the sanding process. Frost rings were classified according to their intensity (low, medium and severe) and position in the ring, initial, and spring as indicated in Figures 2a,b.
TEXT:
[1] (abs) Xylem anomalies that are caused by unusual climate events have long been used to aid cross-dating in tree ring research.
[2] (abs) Here, we analyzed a range of xylem anomalies in a 39-year-old common garden experiment of white spruce (Picea glauca [Moench] Voss) in central Alberta, Canada, designed to investigate local adaptation.
[3] (abs) We extracted wood cores from trees representing 24 provenances covering much of the species range across the Canadian boreal forest.
[4] (abs) Using a double stain and light microscopy analysis, four xylem anomalies and their causes could be distinguished: (1) frost rings indicate issues with synchronizing the onset of growth with the start of the growing season, and were prevalent in young trees; (2) light rings represent thin cell walls caused by an insufficient growing season length, most prevalent in southern sources; (3) blue rings were caused by a failure to complete lignification of new wood due to an early end of the growing season; and (4) double rings represent density fluctuations due to drier than normal summers.
[5] (abs) Local provenances showed the least amount of xylem anomalies, indicating that they are correctly adapted to the environment in which they occur.
[6] (abs) In contrast, trees moved to the test site from other climate regions showed various types of xylem anomalies depending on their origin.
[7] (abs) In particular, populations originating from warmer regions showed an increased presence of latewood anomalies, consistent with a more extensive use of the growing season in the fall.
[8] (abs) We conclude that xylem anomalies may serve as a sensitive early indicator of maladaptation to climate before populations experience tree dieback or mortality.
[9] (abs) They may therefore be useful to monitor the health of natural populations, or to evaluate the success of assisted migration in reforestation to address climate change.
[10] (res) Light rings were detected in 7.6% of the rings, followed by double rings with a 4.2% occurrence rate.
[11] (res) Light and double rings appeared throughout the lifetime of the trees (Figure 3), i.e. their formation was independent of a tree's age or size.
[12] (res) Light rings had latewood tracheids with thinner cell walls than in normal rings.
[13] (res) Double rings were characterized by two latewood bands per rings, interrupted by a layer of wider earlywood-like tracheids.
[14] (res) The least common type of xylem anomaly were blue rings.
[15] (res) We detected blue rings in only 1.6% of the rings.
[16] (res) In all of these cases they occurred in rings formed prior to 2001.
[17] (res) Blue rings were characterized by continuous rows of latewood tracheids whose walls were stained blue (Figure 2d).
[18] (res) The shape or cell wall thickness of these cells did not necessarily differ from "normal" (red stained) tracheids in their proximity.
[19] (res) We next studied the climate variables at the common garden site that could be linked with the occurrence of xylem anomalies.
[20] (res) The formation of frost rings was generally linked to spring temperatures (March to May), but the formation of initial versus spring frost rings was caused by unique temperature patterns (Figure 4).
[21] (res) Initial frost rings were associated to cold minimum temperatures in March (pseudo-R 2 = 0.12, p < 0.001).
[22] (res) By contrast, spring frost rings were associated with mild temperatures in April (R 2 = 0.38, p < 0.001) and May (Figure 4).
[23] (res) FIGURE 3 | Proportion of tree ring anomalies (initial and spring frost rings, light rings, blue rings, and double rings) formed in 1983–2016.
[24] (res) The gray area in the top figure shows the sample size for each year.
[25] (res) Sample size was reduced closer to the tree pith because the corer often missed the earliest rings close to the pith.
[26] (res) A cold beginning of the growing season alone (e.g. 2009 in Figure 5A) or cold end of the growing season alone (e.g. 1992 in Figure 5B) did not induce the formation of light rings.
[27] (res) The monthly variables that were most related to the presence of light rings were high average temperatures in May (R 2 = 0.30, p < 0.001), June (R 2 = 0.31, p < 0.001), and September (R 2 = 0.19, p < 0.001).
[28] (res) Blue rings were associated with cool temperatures in September (R 2 = 0.17, p < 0.001); dry conditions in August also contributed to their formation (R 2 = 0.12, p < 0.001).
[29] (res) Finally, the formation of double rings was favored by warm and dry summers characterized by highly negative climate moisture indices, combined with a sudden increase in precipitation in September.
[30] (res) The highest percentage of double rings was observed in 1998 and 2015 (Figure 3); years with a very dry summer causing the formation of a narrow band of latewood tracheids, followed by a sudden increase in precipitation in September, which led to the transient formation of wider tracheids (Figures 2c, 4).
[31] (res) FIGURE 4 | Relationship between the intensity of xylem anomalies and monthly climate variables at the common garden site.
[32] (res) The values represent the marginal pseudo-R 2 of the generalized linear mixed models of the climate variables that better explained the occurrence of the different anomalies (minimum temperatures for initial and spring frost rings, average temperatures for light and blue rings and climate moisture index for double rings).
[33] (res) The symbol indicates whether the relationship is positive or negative.
[34] (res) Capital letters represent months for the period from March to September.
[35] (res) Correlations between the intensity of xylem anomalies and the climate of the source location of the provenance can aid the interpretation of how populations are adapted to local climate conditions.
[36] (res) The latitude of the seed sources was negatively correlated with the intensity of light, blue, and double rings (Table 2).
[37] (res) Mean annual temperature and the end of the frost free period were positively correlated with these latewood anomalies, meaning that these anomalies were more prevalent in provenances from regions with warm and long growing seasons.
[38] (res) Provenances that showed a higher percentage of blue rings usually came from areas with a late end of the growing season, relatively mild winters and high precipitation levels (Table 2).

SPECIES: T1=Picea glauca (white spruce); T2=Pinus contorta; T3=Pinus nigra

We hypothesized that xylem anomalies can be viewed as symptoms of maladaptation to local growing conditions, and that they can be used as a tool to guide seed transfer in the light of climate change. Specifically, we will interpret xylem anomalies in the light of the climate differences between the source environment of the provenance, and the test environment at the planting site. The trial site is located in the central boreal plains of western Canada, and supports a boreal mixedwood ecosystem on a clay-loam gray luvisol soil. The test site climate is cool and dry, with a mean annual temperature of 0.5°C and mean annual precipitation of 491 mm. Trees from 43 provenances across the Canadian species range were planted in 1982 as 4-year-old seedlings. The experimental design is a randomized complete block design with five blocks and five-tree row plots planted in each block with a 2.5 × 2.5 m spacing. We extracted a wood core from one tree of average height and DBH from each row plot, i.e. one core per block and provenance of the sampling design. Samples were collected during the summer of 2017, with 2016 being the last complete year used for analyses. For every core, we discarded the first few sections to avoid sampling tissue that could have been damage by the sanding process. Frost rings were classified according to their intensity (low, medium and severe) and position in the ring, initial, and spring as indicated in Figures 2a,b.
TEXT:
[39] (res) FIGURE 5 | The formation of light rings was linked to low temperatures at the beginning and end of the growing season.
[40] (res) The graph shows average temperatures in May and June (A) and September (B).
[41] (res) The pink circles represent the proportion of light rings in each year, from 0% (e.g. 1985) to 58% (2004).
[42] (res) The three years with the highest presence of light rings (1996, 2000, and 2004) correspond to the three coldest May and June temperatures of the study period and below-average September temperatures.
[43] (dis) We detected a range of xylem anomalies in the common garden trial, including frost rings.
[44] (dis) These were mostly related to temperatures between March and June, depending on the position of the frost ring.
[45] (dis) Initial frost rings that appeared right at the beginning of the tree ring were associated with low temperatures in March, i.e. before the beginning of the growing season.
[46] (dis) This indicates that the cambium can be damaged by a severe frost before the tree starts that year's growth, so the very first cells produced by the tree will be damaged.
[47] (dis) Spring frost rings on the other hand were related to high temperatures in April and May.
[48] (dis) We suggest that these higher temperatures will advance the start of the growing season for that year, making trees more vulnerable to a late spring frost.
[49] (dis) A similar observation was made by Montwé et al. (2018) who reported that a "false spring" in April contributed to the formation of these frost rings in Pinus contorta trees.
[50] (dis) Frost rings appeared almost exclusively in the first 15 years after planting although favorable climate conditions for their formation persisted in subsequent decades.
[51] (dis) This agrees with previous reports that frost rings are often restricted to smaller trees and stems characterized by small diameters and thin bark.
[52] (dis) A possible explanation for the higher resistance of bigger trees to frost damage is that thicker stems, especially if accompanied by a thicker bark, are able to accumulate more heat so that they can maintain temperatures above freezing in the stem even if outside temperatures drop below 0◦C. In addition, a stand comprised of small saplings will experience more dynamic temperature variations than a closed stand formed by larger trees.
[53] (dis) Light and double rings formed in response to low temperatures and dry conditions, respectively.
[54] (dis) Low temperatures at the beginning of the growing season can limit carbon assimilation reducing the amount of resources available for xylogenesis, while low temperatures at the end of the growing season may restrict carbon mobilization and deposition rates in the cell wall.
[55] (dis) Double rings appear when there is an environmental constraint to xylem formation within the growing season leading to the formation of a band of latewood-like cells.
[56] (dis) This constraint is usually caused by summer droughts (Hoffer and Tardif, 2009; De Micco et al., 2016).
[57] (dis) Trees that are able to expand their growing season for a longer period can take advantage of the good growing conditions in late summer and form a double ring.
[58] (dis) The fact that these xylem anomalies were more frequent in provenances originating from lower latitudes (Table 2 and Supplementary Figure S1) is consistent with a more extensive use of the growing season and a later onset of cold hardiness in these trees at our study site.
[59] (dis) Blue rings are formed as a result of incomplete lignification.
[60] (dis) As such, rings can be linked with low temperatures at the end of the growing season, but lignification is also affected by other factors including water availability.
[61] (dis) Piermattei et al. (2015) observed
[62] (dis) Standard errors of the estimates are given in parenthesis.
[63] (dis) Mean estimates for ecozones with the same letter were not significantly different at p < 0.05, using a Tukey adjustment for multiple comparisons.
[64] (dis) Significant correlations with p < 0.05 after a Holms adjustment for multiple comparisons are indicated in bold. a high proportion of blue rings in years with low temperatures at the end of the growing season.
[65] (dis) In our study, the occurrence of blue rings was correlated with low temperatures in September and low precipitation in August.
[66] (dis) The percentage of blue rings in our study was lower than in studies on Pinus contorta (Montwé et al., 2018; 23% blue rings) and Pinus nigra.
[67] (dis) This may be related to differences in the "life strategies" of pines and spruces (sensu Cuny et al., 2012), and to the inherently short growing season at our boreal planting site.
[68] (dis) Similar to light and double rings, blue rings were more intense in provenances from southern latitudes.
[69] (dis) However, blue rings were also more intense in provenances coming from wetter regions, suggesting that a lack of adaptation to drought might favor the formation of blue rings.
[70] (dis) Our finding that blue rings were primarily formed in the first 10 years of the trees' life agrees with the data of Montwé et al. (2018), who observed significantly lower severity of blue rings with increasing diameter.
[71] (dis) Montwé et al. (2018) suggested that this "may be due to their smaller size and lower heat absorption,..., and their proximity to the soil surface, which is colder due to radiative cooling."
[72] (con) The analysis supports that xylem anomalies can serve as an early indicator of maladaptation to climate before populations experience dieback or mortality.
[73] (con) Local provenances collected near the planting site showed the least overall amount of xylem anomalies.
[74] (con) This indicates that they are correctly adapted to the environment in which they occur, and that xylem anomalies should be at a minimum when planting stock is correctly matched to their optimal growing conditions.
[75] (con) By contrast, provenances from southern regions with longer and warmer growing conditions showed an increased presence of latewood anomalies.
[76] (con) These southern populations showed thin and unlignified cell walls in years when cold temperatures arrived before they could finish the last stages of xylem formation, indicating a potential maladaptation to the shorter growing seasons in the study site.
[77] (con) When such anomalies are observed in assisted migration schemes to address climate change, it would indicate that seed sources have been moved too far poleward or upward in elevation.
[78] (con) Xylem anomalies may also be useful to monitor the health of natural populations.
[79] (con) For example, in this study doublerings were an early sign of growth cessation due to summer drought observed in populations adapted to cooler and wetter environments.
[80] (con) Under climate change toward warmer and drier conditions, this xylem anomaly would serve as an early warning sign of maladaptation before dieback and tree mortality occur.
